title: Census Tract 814.02 — Streeterville / Lakefront, Chicago

movements.text: You arrive at the edge of a city and the edge of a continent. Lake Michigan opens to the east, its shoreline here broken into named pockets — Oak Street Beach, Ohio Street Beach, DuSable Harbor, Monroe Harbor — while the Chicago River and Ogden Slip cut the land to the west and south. The tract sits on less than a square kilometer of it, pressed between water on one side and the dense grid on the other. You are standing in a place defined as much by what surrounds it as by what it contains.

checkpoints.text: A small fraction of the roughly 4,600 housing units here — fewer than two hundred — predate 1940. These oldest structures represent a thin stratum of the tract's residential past, present before any of the large-scale redevelopment that would follow.

The decades between 1960 and 1979 added another five hundred or so units, with the 1960s accounting for the larger share. The 1940s and 1950s left almost no residential footprint — just fifteen units from the forties and none recorded from the fifties.

The 1980s and 1990s together brought roughly 1,330 units, the tract beginning to fill in more consistently. By the close of the twentieth century, a substantial residential density had accumulated along this lakefront strip.

The heaviest construction wave arrived after 2000. The first decade of the century added about 1,075 units; the following decade, ending in 2019, added the single largest cohort — roughly 1,400. The median year built across all units lands at 2002, meaning more than half the housing stock here is less than a quarter century old.
Since 2020, only about two dozen units have been recorded, suggesting the pace of new residential construction has slowed sharply compared with the prior two decades.

Of the roughly 3,950 occupied households, about seven in ten are renter-occupied — a strong majority in a tract where ownership is the exception. The population of around 6,700 has a median age of 35, a relatively young profile. How people leave for work is as varied as the housing itself: the largest single group walks, accounting for more than a quarter of commuters. Working from home claims another quarter. Public transit, driving alone, and cycling together cover most of the rest. That's a rare modal spread for an American urban tract.

Three properties near this address appear in the National Register of Historic Places. The USS Silversides (SS 236), listed in 1972 as a National Historic Landmark and categorized as a structure, sits within about 100 meters of the anchor point. The SS Clipper, also a structure, was listed in 1983 at roughly 150 meters. Further out, at about 1,150 meters, the buildings at 860–880 Lake Shore Drive were listed in 1980 as a building. These three entries are among the oldest named facts in the public record for this immediate area.

paragraphs.text: Walking the streets within about a kilometer of the anchor, you pass an unusually dense commercial layer. Dozens of restaurants and cafes sit within reach, alongside bars, bakeries, and quick-service counters. Eggy's and Caffè Oliva represent the sit-down end of the range; Chipotle, Dunkin', and Potbelly the faster end. Harry Caray's Tavern and Billy Goat Tavern anchor the pub category. For groceries, both Mariano's Fresh Market and Whole Foods Market are mapped in the radius.

The lakefront infrastructure is present in the mapped texture: benches line the shore in large numbers, fountains and shelters appear throughout, and the Columbia Yacht Club sits at the water's edge. Bicycle rentals are available at multiple mapped stations — McClurg Ct & Ohio St among them — and the AMC River East 21 cinema offers an indoor anchor nearby. The Northwestern University Law Library registers as the tract's library presence. A post office — the Streeterville Post Office — appears in the record.
The harbor benches face east. The water is where the address ends.
